extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in late-night television and the production/impact of The Late Late Show with James Corden
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarizing the production, format, recurring segments, reception, and broadcast history of The Late Late Show with James Corden (2015–2023). It documents format choices, notable segments, viewership, awards, and production changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production location and taping schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Taped in front of a studio audience Monday through Thursday afternoons at Television City in Los Angeles, in Studio 56, directly above the Bob Barker Studio (Studio 33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies a conventional late‑night production model: regular weekday taping in a fixed studio location with a live audience; relevant for planning logistics, audience management, and production workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running time and broadcast timeslot
rubrics_metrics.description: Aired in the United States from Monday to Friday nights at 12:37 a.m. ET/PT with a running time of 40 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines format constraints for content, pacing, and segment scheduling; informs expectations for segment length and commercial structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monologue usage and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: While an opening monologue is a staple of the late-night talk show genre, Corden suggested using alternatives to the traditional joke-heavy monologue; the show retained a monologue though it is shorter and not as important an element as the monologue on other late-night shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates a stylistic criterion: favor shorter, less joke-centric monologues or alternative opening devices to differentiate tone and pacing from other hosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview format and guest staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses an interview format similar to The Graham Norton Show, in which all of the night's guests appear on stage simultaneously; guests emerge from the back of the studio and walk through the audience rows. The host sits to the left of the guests (a reversal of the traditional American layout) and does not sit behind a desk but in a swivel chair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes staging and seating choices that shape conversational dynamics and audience engagement: simultaneous-guest seating, host positioning, and audience entrance paths as deliberate format decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: House band and announcer role
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike his predecessors, Corden's Late Late Show has a house band led by Reggie Watts, who also acts as the show's announcer. The band performed lead vocals, keyboards, beatboxing, programming and composed the theme song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a prominent house band as both musical and comedic element; the band contributes to show identity (theme, transitions, live performance moments) and can be integral to recurring bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring segments as core format elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The show features recurring segments such as Carpool Karaoke, Drop the Mic, The Bold and the Lyrical, Riff-Off, Take a Break, Crosswalk the Musical, Spill Your Guts or Fill Your Guts, Flinch, Were You Paying Attention?, Honest Headlines, Emoji News, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring segments define the show's comedic structure and audience expectations; segments should be clearly conceptualized, repeatable, and adaptable to guests. They can drive viral reach and ancillary opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viral potential and online distribution (Carpool Karaoke example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carpool Karaoke is a segment in which James and musical guests sing along while driving on a planned route; these segments have proven popular as viral videos on the show's YouTube channel (e.g., Adele's segment reached 42 million views within five days and 263 million total views as of Feb 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design segments with strong shareable/viral hooks and suitability for online platforms; measure success with view counts, social reach, and the potential for spin-offs or specials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin-offs, specials and franchising potential
rubrics_metrics.description: The popularity of Carpool Karaoke led to an Apple Music series (Carpool Karaoke: The Series) and other producers/stations creating related series or specials (e.g., a Carpool Karaoke primetime special that won a 2016 Emmy for Outstanding Variety Special; Drop the Mic became a series on TBS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful segments can be expanded into standalone programming or specials and become additional revenue/recognition sources; evaluate segments for franchising potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception, awards and industry recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The show received nominations and awards including Primetime Emmy nominations, Creative Arts Emmy wins/nominations, Critics' Choice Television Awards (including wins), and Writers Guild of America nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use awards and industry nominations as measures of critical success and professional recognition when evaluating a show's impact and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewership and ratings as performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured by episodes' viewer numbers and ratings (e.g., debut episode scored 1.66 million viewers; May 20, 2015 episode had 4 million viewers and a 2.5 rating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Nielsen-style viewership and ratings as primary quantitative metrics of audience reach and comparative performance versus peers or historical benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural sensitivity and backlash risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Spill Your Guts or Fill Your Guts' segment received backlash in June 2021 after criticism that the show used traditional Asian foods as 'disgusting' props; a petition demanded apology and cancellation or modification of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate segments for cultural sensitivity and potential offense; avoid using cultural foods or practices as props for humiliation; incorporate diversity-aware review to mitigate backlash risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production adaptability (COVID-19 example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Production was suspended on March 14, 2020; from March 30, 2020 the show resumed with Corden hosting from his garage and communicating via Zoom; later reworked studio formats without guest couches or live audience and intermittent remote hosting as public health required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain flexibility in production design to enable remote/at-home episodes, virtual guest integration, and reconfigured studio setups in response to public-health or other disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format differentiation from predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiators included use of a house band, shorter/less central monologue, simultaneous-guest interview format, host sitting left of guests and not behind a desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate format changes can be used to distinguish a version of a franchise; when producing or evaluating a show, document which elements are intended innovations versus legacy features.
